title: My current workflow — iPad + Claude Code + Steam Deck
author: siendo64
selftext:
There's been a lot of discussion on workflows, so I thought I'd share mine as someone who is a very technically minded game designer, but not an engineer

I've been making games professionally for about 15 years (as a designer or game director). I work for a pretty big publisher, so a lot of what I'm doing is just because I love doing it. I can't really release anything to the world even open source because it would be owned by the publisher.

But, I'm genuinely interested in how I can leverage these new technologies for game dev. I'm not really interested in the art side yet and not sure I will be. Haven't seen anything that I liked. But, I do appreciate the use of LLM for development.

High level, what I decided I wanted to do was

1. Prompt on Claude app
2. Make a PR to github and review
3. Github Action to make a build
4. Script I run on my Steam Deck to download the build
5. Play, test, code review and return to 1

What I tried:

* **Unity with MCP** — Feels clunky. Does so many things in weird and bloated ways. And, Unity is just a bloated engine at this point where I don't need 90% of it's features and they just all get in my way.
* **Unreal with an LLM** – Used the LLM to write C++ for me, it was nice, but I didn't feel like I was actually faster than being able to hook up my own blueprints or work with the editor. Also, similar situation to Unity... it's just so bloated and built as something for everyone at this point
* **Godot** — Builds under 2 minutes, but minimum export bundle is 30MB and the scene system boggles the LLM. I can get good core logic out of it in GDScript, but Claude has no idea how to architect something in Godot well. Makes weird assumptions about how the engine works that are just wrong. Maybe this gets better with better docs in the training data, but it felt like I was so far from it being usable.
* **Bevy** — Genuinely pleasant to work in with an LLM. I really like the ECS paradigm and how it can really open up some interesting creative space when we think about games in that way. I really don't like writing Rust myself though, so it was nice to get the LLM to do it. haha. CI started at 45 minute builds. Got it down to 15 with mold/sccache, still too long to iterate from an iPad. No path to consoles either.
* **Phaser, Three.js, Babylon.js** — Fine for browsers. I'm not shipping to browsers. I got my gameplay really far with Babylon, but at a certain point it just doesn't know what to do anymore because the code gets so bloated. I probably could have pushed through, but it felt like too much effort to never be able to ship to a Switch one day.

All of these are built for someone sitting at a desk with the editor open. That isn't my workflow.

What I'm doing now: plain C11 with Sokol (window/GPU/audio) and HandmadeMath. One [build.sh](http://build.sh), no CMake, no package manager. GitHub Actions builds a Linux release on every push, and a small zenity picker on the Deck lets me grab any PR build. Binary is 300k, full build under 30 seconds, CI to playable on the Deck is a couple of minutes.

The architecture has gotten super simple. The earlier version of this had a custom entity-component system and a planned JS scripting layer, and the LLM got lost in both. Claude had no training data on my specific abstractions even though I fully documented the architecture in [CLAUDE.md](http://CLAUDE.md), so it kept patching symptoms instead of fixing root causes, and the fixes piled up. Cut all of that. Now it's plain structs and straightforward C, and Claude handles it much better.

Apologies if this got long, but wanted to share my experience with y'all in more detaul. I've mentioned what I'm doing in a couple of comments elsewhere and got called a dumbass for "rebuilding the wheel." Mods deleted it, but it still sat with me and I wanted to explain my experience to people. And honestly, I don't think I'm looking for a wheel right now. I'm looking for a creative workflow that fits how I want to work with an LLM and the way I want to work to make new creative and cool stuff.

Curious on other people's experience and workflows as well. Especially with the Steam Deck as a dev machine. I know there's lots of dev tools, but I haven't really gotten into them yet.

comments.author: johnreno
comments.body: I use Three.js with a NW.js build for Linux which works really well for Steam Deck - including controller support and vibration. It's also a good machine to test against slightly weaker specs to find any bottlenecks, especially with Three.js because you really need to hardcode performance tricks that you take for granted in other engines.

comments.author: mistafisha
comments.body: Since HTML, CSS, and JavaScript can be wrapped for mobile publishing, I wouldn't rule out using "browser code."

replies.author: siendo64
replies.body: Yah. This is something I've been seriously considering. I think the idea that I wouldn't be able to ship something to a console eventually is the only thing holding me back. Been trying to look at every avenue that could eventually lead to that at the moment.

comments.author: Frolicks
comments.body: When you review builds how often are you catching bugs? I'm doing a terminal gui game that connects to a space-time DB backend and most of iterations are catching simple bugs that I feel like the llm could've caught itself if it examined the output more critically. Most of my effort is trying to set up this recursive self improvement

replies.author: siendo64
replies.body:
It depends on the underlying tech I've used. Godot it was non-stop really simple oversights. When I had a custom ECS system, it did the same thing. Now that I've made things a lot more straightforward it's much better.

I really think it has to do with the training data. When I try to be creative and build some new kind of architecture it makes really bad assumptions on how things are working without bothering to investigate how it actually works. I guess the context window is just too large for it.

I've seen some people using LittleJS, I may try that out since it's something I could just include for complete context.

replies.author: Frolicks
replies.body:
Nice very cool. Just curious what is your genre / problem space? I'm doing a tower defense - ish management thing, which should be deterministic, so im still pursuing that self improvement loop with the llm. 

I considered doing something more physics based games, but haven't yet since I figure these issues would be worse

replies.author: siendo64
replies.body: My stuff is more traditional top down or fixed camera adventure/rpg type stuff but in 3D. So, definitely not doing anything with crazy physics or really high amount of entities.

comments.author: rjyo
comments.body:
The plain C + Sokol move is exactly right for LLM-driven dev. Same path here. Any custom abstraction or DSL the model has no training data for, it just patches symptoms forever no matter how thorough your [CLAUDE.md](http://CLAUDE.md) is. Cutting the custom ECS was probably the highest-leverage decision in this writeup.

  
For the not-at-a-desk part of your loop — I built an iOS terminal app called Moshi specifically for this kind of workflow (iPad/iPhone SSH to a dev box, run Claude Code remotely). Uses Mosh protocol so the session survives sleep and network switches, has a Claude shortcut tab, and push notifications when an agent finishes so you don't keep tabbing back. If you ever want to skip the Claude app → PR → CI hop for quick iteration, SSH from iPad to a small VPS or Pi running Claude Code CLI gives you a much tighter loop, and you can rsync builds straight to the Deck.

  
What's your asset workflow looking like — procedural for now, or did you find a tool that holds up?

replies.author: siendo64
replies.body: I use Termius of SSH when I need to from my ipad. But, it's not ideal. I find typing into a console with the ipad is really tricky. There's things I do in command line that I just cant do. Ctrl + R, Up arrow, just basic stuff like that is so unintuitive.

comments.author: CursehoundDev
comments.body:
I've actually found Claude (Opus 4.6 at least) to be pretty solid for Godot. I've been playing around with a few game concept ideas and I've found Godot by far the easiest for it to work with, as it's able to build scenes and game logic without needing MCP or other integrations.


Highly recommend building out a Claude.md and steering documentation, as it makes it way easier to stay on the rails. Every time I see it make a mistake or use a clumsy pattern, I have it update it's internal documents with notes to avoid those in the future, and now after a few weeks I've got my setup refined enough that I'm able to put together pretty functional prototypes without much more than plan mode.


Taking that idea from prototype to full game still takes a lot of work, of course, but on more than one occasion I've had a game idea while out doing things, put that idea into the Claude mobile app and worked through a plan, and then by the time I get home I've got a playable build to mess around with. It's honestly kind of shocking

replies.author: siendo64
replies.body: Are you working with the code base over multiple different chats? Or is it just a single chat? I usually work by picking off a feature I want to work on and then shipping that with Claude. I've found after like 3-4 different game systems it really makes simple and frustrating mistakes

replies.author: CursehoundDev
replies.body:
I try to keep it to one chat per feature, but sometimes I'll get carried away and end up doing a few in a row. The size of the codebase impacts that a lot as well, with larger ones needing more frequent compactions or resets.


A brand new prototype can handle one chat for quite a while, but my largest project has recently passed 150k lines of code and I have to be much more specific about how what context I include and the instructions I give it.


Making use of plan mode has been a life saver as well, because that lets me formulate and polish up an idea to pre-empt those mistakes a bit, and then you get a fresh context window when you approve the plan so it stays much more on topic

comments.author: Trashy_io
comments.body:
Build around limitations or build or find tools for bottle necks. Never trust the LLM to fix something correctly always at the very least skim what it changes you'll find it changes a lot of unnecessary stuff. 

I have a free file system as well you can run on claude its basically set up for any model to track the progress in a number of ways in plain text I call it context mapping, I'm not super technical when it comes to terminology but in a sense that what it does and for larger projects it is a must to have something like this, it should be the first and last thing your agents touch most prompts unless making tiny edits.

Not over loading the LLM youll get a feel for it but keep it to one major change or 3-5 smaller changes per prompt early on its more lenient but almost always drops quality of code going over that amount.

comments.author: rjyo
comments.body:
Yeah those exact gaps are why I built Moshi. Long-press space gives you a trackpad-style cursor for arrow keys, and Ctrl+R, Esc, Tab, pipe, etc are one-tap toolbar buttons you can reorder or hide. There is also a Claude shortcuts tab so you skip typing out the slash commands.

  
The other Termius pain on iPad — disconnect when the screen locks or wifi switches — Moshi runs over Mosh, so the session just survives sleep and network switches. Hasn't dropped on me in months.

replies.author: siendo64
replies.body: Ah cool. I’m gonna have to check it out. TY!

comments.author: Deep_Ad1959
comments.body: the part where Claude ignored CLAUDE.md when you had a custom ECS is the most important takeaway in this whole writeup and most people miss it. CLAUDE.md doesn't compete with the model's training prior, if you describe a custom abstraction in 800 tokens but it has millions of plain-struct C examples baked into its weights, it will write plain structs by default and patch over your abstraction no matter how thorough the doc is. the win wasn't really 'cutting the ECS', it was 'aligning the codebase with the training distribution so CLAUDE.md doesn't have to fight a losing battle'. same reason vanilla react beats your home-grown framework in agent flows, vanilla python beats your domain DSL, plain SQL beats your ORM wrapper. CLAUDE.md is for principles and invariants, not for re-teaching the model your custom paradigm. written with s4lai
